title: Importing the base mesh
description: Import the base mesh FBX into Blender, set its scale back to 1, and see why it needs more geometry before it can be rigged.
content:
Rigging starts with a mesh to rig. In this short part you'll bring a simple character base mesh into Blender from an FBX file, fix the tiny scale it comes in at, and look at its wireframe to see what it's missing before it can bend. You'll need Blender (the video uses Blender 2.90) and the base mesh FBX file from the exercise.

Import the FBX

  1. Start a new scene and delete the cube. 0:09 Select the default cube and press X to delete it.

  2. Choose File → Import → FBX. 0:14 FBX is the format the base mesh comes in.

  3. Pick the base mesh and import it. 0:19 Find the FBX file you downloaded, leave all the import settings as they are and click Import FBX.

Fix the scale

  1. Check the object's scale. 0:33 The model comes in very small. Open the sidebar at the right of the viewport (N) and select the model in the Outliner (it's called pCube1) so the sidebar's Item tab shows its transform. Its scale is 0.01 on every axis: it was scaled down before it was exported.

  2. Set the scale to 1. 0:47 Click in the first Scale field and drag down across all three to edit them together, type 1 and press Return. Zoom out and the model is now a good size to start working with.

    The video reads the 1.68 m in Dimensions Z as the character's height. The model came in rotated 90° on X, though, and the sidebar measures dimensions along the object's own axes, so here Y (11.5 m) is the height and Z (1.68 m) is the depth from front to back.

Check that the mesh can bend

  1. Look at the wireframe. 1:27 Switch the viewport to wireframe shading. The base mesh isn't ready to be rigged yet: it doesn't have the vertices it needs to deform like a character.

  2. See what's missing. 1:41 To bend an arm at the elbow, there have to be vertices at the elbow. Without them, moving the hand just stretches a straight line from the shoulder's vertices to the hand's. The next parts add edge loops and vertices where the character needs to bend.

Wrap-up

The base mesh is in your scene at a scale of 1, standing in a T-pose. It's still too simple to bend: in the next parts you'll mirror it and add edge loops where it needs to deform.

Transcript

From speech to text.

0:00 Okay, so to get started with rigging, we are going to import a base mesh that's been started, and we're going to apply a rig to it. So I'm going to go ahead and delete this default cube, press X to delete, and we're going to go to File → Import, and we're going to go down to FBX, and that's the file type that we'll be importing. and I've already got that file here in a folder so I'm going to just leave all of these settings as they are, click import FBX and you'll notice that it comes in really small and if we were to just pop out this side panel and just select our object here in the outliner to make sure that the item tab shows up we can see that it's actually been scaled before we brought it in. So if we want to correct the scale all we have to do is select all of these at once by dragging across all three and pressing one and return and that basically makes the scale one so if I zoom out now what you'll notice is that the model is the proper size to start working with and you can see on the right in the dimensions that the Z or the vertical axis is 1.68 meters that's actually pretty accurate to how tall a person is. Obviously people are different heights, but this is a good

1:19 size to work in. So just correct that scale before you get started. Okay, now we need to take a look at whether our base mesh is ready to be rigged. And if we go to wireframe, what you'll notice is that it's actually not ready. And what we're missing are vertices to allow this mesh to deform like a character might. For instance, if you want to bend the arm at the elbow, what we'll notice is that there's actually no vertices here to make that bend possible. So if you move the hand, it will draw a line between these vertices and wherever the kind of hand vertices end up. So what we will need to do is go through and add edge loops and vertices in strategic locations where we know that we'll want to deform our model.

2:11 So let's go ahead and get started with that.
